title: The Courtyard of Five Shields

narrative.arrival: You step out into a sunlit courtyard paved with massive stone shields. Three stand tall and two lie flat, locked edge to edge without a mortar gap.
narrative.sealed: The stone shields sink slightly with a rumble, revealing golden tracks underneath. The hidden seams glow, and the path to the keep is unlocked.

inscription: The courtyard floor is five identical stone shields fitted together with no gaps: three stand upright side by side in the top row, and two lie flat end to end in the bottom row. Walking all the way around the outside of the courtyard measures 66 cubits. How far is it around one shield?

parts.prompt: Walking all the way around the outside of the five fitted shields measures 66 cubits. How far is it around one shield?

misconceptions.probe: You shared the outside walk equally among the shields. Does every side of every shield lie on the outside of the courtyard?
That is the walk around the whole courtyard. What is the question asking about instead?
Look at the seam where the standing shields meet the lying ones: what does that shared line tell you about a long side and a short side?
Which lengths do we know as numbers, and which do we know only as a relationship between shapes?

l0: Boots ready, notebook open. Before we trace any edges, are we looking for the walk around the whole courtyard or the walk around a single stone shield?
My blueprint has room for measurements and for things we know from the arrangement. What does the inscription tell us as a number, and what does the shape tell us?
The Stonemason set these shields edge to edge. Where do the standing shields touch the lying ones, and what can we say about that line?
l1: I'll hold the blueprint still. At the place where the standing shields meet the flat shields, what does the shared seam tell us about their sides?
Lemma is sorting the Deck beside the blueprint. Is there a card that could help us look at something the rows of shields share?
The Stonemason's ruler is missing, so we can choose our own unit. Could a small unit measure both a short side and a long side with no leftover?

l2.text: The middle seam joins three short sides to two long sides. Mark a short side as 2 units and a long side as 3 units on the blueprint. How do the sides on the outer border fit together?

l4.statement: Two identical squares side by side make a rectangle whose outside walk is 36 cubits. How far is it around one square?
l4.l3: Count how many square sides lie on the outside of the rectangle, then share the 36 cubits among them. Multiply by 4.

l3.text: Trace the outer border in units across the top, bottom and sides. Use its length to find the cubits in a unit. What distance does that give for the walk around a single shield?

Find the distance around a single stone shield

lookBack.prompt: Five separate shields have five outside walks. Add them up and compare with the courtyard’s 66. How many cubits of shield edge are hidden inside the courtyard?
Suppose the courtyard walk were 44 cubits instead. How far around one shield then?
Measure in cubits directly. The courtyard’s left edge is one long side plus one short side, and that is half of one shield’s walk. How many cubits is the left edge?

codex.theorem: Shared edges cancel (perimeter of compound shapes)
codex.oneLine: When shapes share an edge, that edge disappears from the outside walk, once for each shape.
